The string/bin count cap (line 62) bounds td.count but does not tie it to the actual signature data-region length; full protection against an OOB read inside headerPut would rely on header-region validation performed at load time outside this fragment.

The return value of headerPut is discarded via the (void) cast at line 69; a failed put is silent, but no in-fragment security consequence (beyond a likely fail-closed signature verification) is demonstrable.
No NULL producer for h or hi is shown in the fragment, so NULL-dereference of headerIsEntry/headerPut is not a confirmable finding.

verdict.summary: The uid parse accepts negative values: the guard at line 28 rejects errno/parse errors and values above INT_MAX but imposes no lower bound, so an attacker-supplied FILENAME_UID such as "-1" passes and is cast at line 34 (uid = (uid_t)val) into a wrapped 32-bit uid_t (e.g., 4294967295). That corrupted value is then used to set the created dump directory's ownership at lines 50/54/63/70 and 110, corrupting the ownership/access-control decision. The absent one-statement fix is a val < 0 check in the line-28 condition.

evidence.reason: Sink of CWE-195: val originates from strtol(uid_str) at line 26 where uid_str is attacker-controlled entry-point data (FILENAME_UID); the guard at line 28 admits val in [LONG_MIN, INT_MAX] because it rejects only errno!=0, endptr==uid_str, *endptr!='\0', and INT_MAX<val, leaving every negative value admitted. The degenerate witness "-1" passes all four conditions, so (uid_t)(-1) wraps to 4294967295 and is consumed as the dump-directory owner by try_dd_create(base_dir_name, problem_id, uid) at line 50 (also 54/63/70) and dd_create_basic_files(dd, uid, NULL) at line 110. The absent fix statement is a val < 0 term added to the line-28 condition, which would exclude the entire [LONG_MIN, -1] failure set.

assumptions: uid_t is 32-bit unsigned on the target Linux platform, so casting a negative long wraps modulo 2^32.

try_dd_create and dd_create_basic_files use the uid argument to set the created dump directory's ownership (name- and parameter-implied semantics); the value is therefore a security-relevant access-control consumer.
str_is_correct_filename rejects path separators, traversal components, and other disallowed characters, so the type (line 13) and name (line 82) validations cover their respective path sinks.
limitations: concat_path_file(base_dir_name, problem_id) at line 113 dereferences a possibly-NULL base_dir_name: line 49 explicitly branches on NULL and lines 51-71 handle it via fallback directories, but NULL is produced only by an unshown caller, so per the NULL-producer rule this is not a confirmable CWE-476 in-fragment; it would be a crash (DoS) for callers passing NULL.

copy_file(value->content, dest, ...) at line 92 copies an unvalidated, attacker-supplied source path; the disclosure impact depends on unshown daemon privileges and directory mode, and no clean one-statement fix form is visible, so it is demoted.
log_info at line 46 prints uid_t with %d (sign mismatch) and base_dir_name with %s when NULL; benign in practice, not a finding.

The negative-uid corruption affects ownership integrity/availability (invalid owner, chown no-change sentinel) but grants no capability beyond the already-admitted uid range [0, INT_MAX], so severity is low.

verdict.summary: smacker_read_header never bounds the file-supplied smk->frames (line 13): the guard at line 27 only logs 'Too many frames' and never returns, so all 32-bit values proceed. At line 29, 'smk->frames * 4' wraps modulo 2^32 (witness frames=0x40000001 yields a 4-byte allocation), and the loop at line 33 writes one 4-byte get_le32 per frame into frm_size, producing a heap out-of-bounds write at line 34. Independently, 'smk->treesize + 16' at line 71 wraps (treesize=0xFFFFFFFF gives a 15-byte allocation), and the 16-byte header write at lines 82-85 overruns it at line 85. The absent one-statement fix is 'return -1;' after the av_log at line 28; the treesize wrap additionally lacks an input bound before the '+16'.

evidence.reason: Heap OOB write (CWE-787). smk->frames comes from get_le32(pb) at line 13 with residual range 0..0xFFFFFFFF; the only guard, line 27 'if(smk->frames > 0xFFFFFF)', has a log-only body (line 28) and admits every value. The capacity is computed at line 29 'av_malloc(smk->frames * 4)' in 32-bit arithmetic: for the admitted witness frames=0x40000001 it wraps to 4 bytes, so the loop at line 33 (i < frames, max index frames-1) writes bytes 4..7 at i=1 and continues for 0x3FFFFFFF more iterations, all past the 4-byte allocation. The strict '<' bound does not help because the capacity uses the same wrapped product. Absent fix: 'return -1;' after the av_log at line 28, which would exclude all frames > 0xFFFFFF and the entire failure set. Secondary CWE-190: the wrap in 'smk->frames * 4' is what makes the small allocation possible.

Heap OOB write (CWE-787). smk->treesize from get_le32(pb) at line 18 has the full 32-bit domain; for the witness treesize=0xFFFFFFFF, line 71 'av_malloc(smk->treesize + 16)' wraps to a 15-byte allocation and line 72 sets extradata_size=15. The guard at line 73 tests only NULL (the allocation is non-NULL), so it is bypassed (wrong-target drift: pointer vs size). This write stores int32[3] at offset 12, covering bytes 12-15, with byte 15 beyond the 15-byte object; lines 82-84 are in-bounds but the cumulative 16-byte header overruns. Absent fix: an input bound on treesize before the '+16' (e.g., reject treesize > 0xFFFFFFEF).

assumptions: smk->frames and smk->treesize hold the full 32-bit unsigned values returned by get_le32(pb) (lines 13, 18), so 'smk->frames * 4' and 'smk->treesize + 16' are evaluated in 32-bit arithmetic and wrap modulo 2^32.
av_malloc returns a non-NULL buffer of the requested (wrapped) size for the small witness sizes 4 and 15 bytes, so the overflow writes are into a live heap object rather than a NULL pointer.

Lines 29-31 are outside the line 27 if-block (per indentation), so the allocations execute unconditionally; even if read as inside the block, no return exists and the loops at 33-36 would still execute, which does not change the verdict.
limitations: The magic check at line 10 has no body/return, so non-SMACK files continue parsing, but no security-relevant sink is shown downstream of it — robustness only.

The 'if (!st)' at line 39 (and the unchecked av_new_stream at line 59) can lead to NULL dereferences at lines 40/60, but the NULL producer is fixed-size allocation failure, not attacker-reachable per the class rules.

get_buffer at line 77 is called with an out-of-bounds pointer (extradata + 16) and size -1 for the treesize wrap witness; its exact negative-size behavior is not derivable from the fragment, so that write path is demoted and the extradata overflow is instead evidenced by the line 82-85 header writes.
smk->frm_flags writes at line 36 fail only when av_malloc(smk->frames) at line 30 fails (NULL deref) — subsumed by the same unguarded-frames root cause as the primary finding.
pts_inc negation at line 49 and av_log format strings (numeric %i only) have no confirmed security sink in the shown fragment.

verdict.summary: The privileged SR write at line 9 (gen_helper_store_sr) is gated by the supervisor check CHK_SV at line 7, which raises an illegal-instruction exception for non-privileged guest execution before the store; CONFIG_USER_ONLY builds trap via GEN_PRIV at line 4. No in-fragment capacity or index derivation supports an OOB on cpu_gpr, and no other security sink is demonstrable. The fragment is the patched counterpart.

assumptions: CHK_SV (line 7) is the SH4 supervisor-mode check that raises an illegal-instruction exception when the current execution mode is not privileged (macro defined outside the fragment); in supervisor mode the mtsr write to SR is the intended legitimate operation.
tcg_const_tl (line 8) never returns NULL (QEMU aborts on allocation failure), so the use of t0 at line 9 is safe.
In CONFIG_USER_ONLY builds, line 4 (GEN_PRIV) unconditionally raises a privilege exception and lines 6-10 are not compiled.
limitations: An out-of-bounds read on cpu_gpr[rS(ctx->opcode)] (line 9) cannot be confirmed: neither the capacity of cpu_gpr nor the extraction range of the rS()/SR() macros is declared in the fragment, and the OOB rule requires an in-fragment capacity declaration and an in-fragment numeric derivation.

The exact bit-level semantics of CHK_SV (which SR.MD/tb_flags condition triggers the exception) are defined outside the fragment; the guard's role is inferred from its name and the parallel GEN_PRIV usage in the user-only branch.

verdict.summary: display_dollar() contains the one-statement negative-column clamp at line 3 (col = col_arg < 0 ? 0 : col_arg), which maps every col_arg in [INT_MIN, -1] to 0 before the mb_head_off(p, p + col) read at line 18, fully excluding the only in-fragment confirmable failure (reading before the line start). No other dangerous operation is confirmable: past-end reads depend on an unshown line capacity and an unshown oversized-column producer.

assumptions: ml_get_curline() at line 17 returns a pointer to the start of the current line, making p the object's lower boundary.
colnr_T is signed, as established by the `col_arg < 0` comparison at line 3.
mb_head_off(p, p + col) reads only within [p, p + col] and returns at most col, so w_cursor.col = col - off cannot underflow.
ml_get_curline() returns non-NULL (no in-fragment NULL producer).
limitations: A positive col_arg exceeding the line length would make p + col point past the line's NUL, but the line buffer's capacity and any in-fragment producer of such a column are not shown, so no OOB read can be confirmed.

verdict.summary: The JNI entry point passes the attacker-controlled cpIndex directly into getFieldAt with no bounds validation, so a negative or out-of-range constant-pool index reaches the callee's array-style entry lookup and causes an out-of-bounds read in the JVM.

evidence.reason: cpIndex is an entry-point JNI input of type jint with residual range equal to the full signed 32-bit domain [INT_MIN, INT_MAX]: the fragment (lines 1-5) contains no conditional or validation constraining it. At line 4 it is forwarded unmodified to getFieldAt, which by its standard semantics performs a constant-pool entry lookup indexed by cpIndex against the bounded entry array of the pool referenced by constantPoolOop (valid index space [0, count)). The single path from the parameter to the sink passes zero guards, so failing values such as cpIndex = -1 or any value >= count are fully admitted. The Fix-Presence Scan shows the absent one-statement fix: a bounds check before the call, e.g. if (cpIndex < 0 || cpIndex >= constantPoolCount) return NULL;, or the unsigned-cast comparison form. Without it, a negative or oversized index reaches the callee's array access, producing the CWE-125 out-of-bounds read; the exact overread magnitude depends on the unshown constantPoolCount, which is recorded as a limitation.

assumptions: constantPoolOop references a valid J9 constant pool whose entry array is indexed from 0 with a non-negative count (standard J9/JNI semantics of the constant pool).
getFieldAt performs array-subscript-style constant-pool entry lookup by cpIndex, per the standard semantics implied by its name and the J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_NO_CLASS_LOAD context.
cpIndex arriving through the JNI native-method boundary is externally supplied and therefore attacker-controlled, since the fragment shows no producer or validation for it.
limitations: The exact capacity constantPoolCount and the constant pool's memory layout are not shown in the fragment, so the precise magnitude of the out-of-bounds read rests on standard J9 constant-pool semantics; this caps confidence near the lower band.
Only an out-of-bounds read is claimed; no memory-write, NULL-dereference, or injection mechanism is asserted.

verdict.summary: JNI wrapper passes an unvalidated, attacker-controlled jint cpIndex directly to getFieldAt, which indexes the ConstantPool, with no bounds or equality check on the index. Any cpIndex outside the pool bounds reaches the sink, enabling out-of-bounds access.

evidence.snippet: return getFieldAt(env, constantPoolOop, cpIndex, J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_JIT_COMPILE_TIME | J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_NO_THROW_ON_FAIL);
evidence.reason: cpIndex is an entry-point jint with the full INT_MIN..INT_MAX domain (no shown constraint) and is passed unchecked at line 4 to getFieldAt, whose name-implied semantics index the finite ConstantPool. The fragment contains no bound/equality check, so any negative or >= pool_length index is admitted by the empty guard set and reaches the sink, causing an out-of-bounds access (CWE-787). The absent one-statement fix is a bounds check on cpIndex (e.g., 'if (cpIndex < 0 || cpIndex >= length)') before the call.

assumptions: getFieldAt consumes cpIndex as an index into a finite ConstantPool (name-implied semantics of the callee).
limitations: The concrete ConstantPool length/capacity is not declared within this fragment; it lives inside the unshown getFieldAt, so the exact numeric overflow magnitude cannot be derived from the shown code. Confirmation relies on the name-implied pool indexing semantics plus the total absence of any bound on cpIndex, capping confidence in the 0.5-0.64 band.

verdict.summary: flashsv2_prime ignores the return status of the first inflate() call on attacker-controlled compressed data and unconditionally returns success (line 30), so a corrupt or empty input stream leaves s->zstream in a failed/undefined state that the caller treats as successfully primed (fail-open status-handling flaw).

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled entry-point input src/size (lines 1, 8-9, no shown constraint) is passed to inflate at line 12; zlib's standard semantics return Z_DATA_ERROR/Z_BUF_ERROR for invalid or empty deflate data, and that failure domain is fully admitted because no guard tests the return value (the only checks, lines 13-14 on deflateInit and lines 21-24 on inflateReset, are bystanders constraining different calls — Guard-Identity Audit wrong-target drift). The discarded status then reaches the unconditional success return at line 30, reporting a primed stream after a failed decompression step; the absent one-statement fix is a return-status check such as 'if (inflate(&s->zstream, Z_SYNC_FLUSH) != Z_OK) return AVERROR_UNKNOWN;'. Degenerate witnesses size==0 (Z_BUF_ERROR) and non-zlib bytes in src (Z_DATA_ERROR) both fall through to return 0. Primary CWE-754: improper check of the inflate result causing fail-open status on an attacker-reachable security-relevant step.

assumptions: zlib standard semantics: inflate() returns Z_OK/Z_STREAM_END on progress, Z_DATA_ERROR on invalid deflate data, Z_BUF_ERROR when no progress is possible, and never writes beyond avail_out (lines 11, 28) — this bounds all in-fragment memory writes, so no OOB is claimed.

The capacities of s->tmpblock and s->deflate_block, and the value range of s->block_size/s->deflate_block_size, are established only in unshown decoder init code; no in-fragment capacity exists to support a memory-safety finding.
limitations: The ultimate memory-safety/decoder impact of continuing with the failed zlib state occurs in the unshown caller (flashsv2_decode_frame), so the confirmed finding is the fail-open status flaw (CWE-754), not a demonstrable in-fragment out-of-bounds access.
A negative 'size' would widen to a large uInt avail_in (line 9), but the backing-buffer guarantee for src is caller-side and unshown; treated as a limitation.
The second unchecked inflate at line 29 consumes deflate()'s own valid output, so an attacker-triggerable failure there is not independently confirmable from the shown code.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability within the fragment. limitations: Potential out-of-bounds on utility_inc[i] (L10) or utility[i] (L8) cannot be confirmed because the array capacities are not shown in the fragment.

Signed integer overflow in elbg->numCB*elbg->utility[i] (L7) and inc += elbg->utility[i] (L8) is possible, but no security-relevant consumer of the overflowed value is demonstrated in the shown code, so it is treated as a robustness/defensive-hardening concern (potential CWE-190) rather than a confirmed finding.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. verdict.summary: The signer-name acceptance decision is fully guarded: the boundary check at line 20 (exact-length match or whitespace after the trusted-name prefix), combined with strncmp semantics at line 19, makes shorter-prefix admission unreachable, and the OR short-circuit ensures isspace(signature_name[len]) at line 20 is only evaluated when len < strlen(signature_name), so the index is always in-bounds. assumptions: cert_name is a static array of NUL-terminated trusted-signer strings with ARRAYSIZE entries (table contents not shown).
GetSignatureName returns either NULL or a valid NUL-terminated string; NULL is handled at line 12.

The OR short-circuit at line 20 guarantees isspace receives an in-bounds character.

limitations: cert_name contents are unshown; an empty entry (len == 0) would make strncmp match any name and shift the boundary test onto the first character of the signer name — cannot be confirmed or excluded from the shown code.

The whitespace-boundary clause admits signer names equal to a trusted name plus trailing whitespace; this is the fragment's own visible design, and whether an attacker can obtain such a code-signing subject is not demonstrable in-fragment.
Log injection via a signer name containing CR/LF reaching uprintf at line 25 was considered but demoted: the format is a literal and hostile subject issuance is outside the shown code.
signature_name is never freed (memory leak) — a robustness concern, not a security finding.
isspace with a negative char value (UTF-8 bytes >= 0x80) is technically UB per the ctype contract, but no security consequence is derivable from the shown code.

verdict.summary: The attacker-controlled logout URL is validated by oidc_validate_post_logout_url (lines 27-33) before it can reach the post_logout_redirect_uri open-redirect sink; the NULL/empty case substitutes the trusted default_slo_url, and id_token_hint is escaped. oidc_debug(r, "enter (url=%s)", url) writes the raw attacker URL to a debug log; this is a debug-only sink and not the discriminating fix, so it is not treated as a confirmed CWE-117 finding.

verdict.summary: The in-loop buffer access is fully bounded by `i < 512 - 16` (line 24), keeping the maximum reached index b[i+7] at 502 within the 512-byte stack buffer; this is the fixed counterpart.

verdict.summary: The fragment is the fixed counterpart of the pair. Every dangerous operation is covered by a protective statement that passes the Guard-Identity Audit: line 14 `if (den && num)` excludes den==0 and num==0 from the denominator of the line 15 av_rescale (the only demonstrably reachable divide-by-zero), and line 45 `frame_size >= 0` excludes all negative values before the line 46 av_frac_add. compute_frame_duration initializes *num/*den (its FFmpeg semantics); the existence of the line 14 guard evidences that zero outputs are possible.
get_audio_frame_size can return a negative frame size (evidenced by the line 45 `frame_size >= 0` check).
AV_TIME_BASE is the FFmpeg constant 1,000,000 and AV_NOPTS_VALUE is INT64_MIN, used for the comparisons on lines 6, 8, 19, 24, 26.

All in-fragment int64 products ((int64_t)time_base.den * frame_size / frame_rate_base, num * time_base.den, den * time_base.num, AV_TIME_BASE * time_base.num) are bounded by (2^31-1)^2 < INT64_MAX and cannot overflow.

A potential divide-by-zero inside the unshown callee get_audio_frame_size (e.g., bits_per_coded_sample == 0) is outside the fragment and cannot be confirmed from the shown code.
`-pkt->duration` at line 27 is undefined only for duration == INT64_MIN, whose production is not derivable from any shown statement; timestamp-only consequence in any case.
Negative frame_size without the line 45 guard would only corrupt timestamp accounting, not memory safety; the guard is present regardless.
No memory, injection, crypto, file/access-control, or authn/authz sink exists in the fragment; all dangerous operations reduce to arithmetic over timestamps.

verdict.summary: Signed 32-bit integer overflow in the multiplication elbg->numCB * elbg->utility[i] on line 6, which is computed in int and only then compared to the int64_t elbg->error. A product of 2^31 or larger wraps, feeding a corrupted value into the comparison that drives cumulative utility (utility_inc) used for codebook cell selection. The one-statement fix — casting an operand to int64_t, e.g. (int64_t)elbg->numCB * elbg->utility[i] — is absent.

evidence.reason: numCB and utility[i] are unconstrained int values (full signed 32-bit domain; no shown bound). The int*int product on line 6 overflows once numCB*utility[i] >= 2^31 (e.g. numCB=65536, utility[i]=65536 wraps to 0), and the wrapped int is sign-extended and compared against int64_t elbg->error, corrupting the branch that accumulates inc into utility_inc[i] (lines 7-8) which drives codebook selection. The loop guard on line 5 only bounds the index i and does not constrain the operands' magnitude (wrong-target drift); the comparison itself evaluates after the overflow. The absent one-statement fix is widening an operand, e.g. (int64_t)elbg->numCB * elbg->utility[i]. Primary CWE-190 (integer overflow) with the corrupted value consumed by a security-relevant comparison.

assumptions: numCB and utility[i] are 32-bit signed int and can reach values whose product exceeds 2^31; both are codec/entry-point-derived with no magnitude bound visible in the fragment.
utility_inc and utility arrays are sized to numCB, so the i indexing is in-bounds (loop of numCB iterations).
limitations: The exact magnitudes of numCB and utility[i] that reach this function are set by callers/bitstream data not shown, so the overflow witness relies on the operands' full int domain rather than a shown producer.

The direct in-fragment consequence is a corrupted comparison/decision (logic/codebook state), not an immediate out-of-bounds access; downstream memory impact of the wrong utility_inc is outside this fragment.

verdict.summary: The logout URL (attacker-controlled request parameter, line 7) is validated before use in the redirect sink (line 94). The decisive protective statement is the CR/LF rejection check at line 53, which blocks HTTP header splitting by excluding any url containing '\n' or '\r' on every user-controlled path. The hostname cross-check (lines 39-41) also constrains open-redirect destinations. No unprotected dangerous operation remains.

The hostname check (lines 39-41) uses bidirectional substring matching (strstr); because both directions must hold it effectively requires hostname equality, and a NULL hostname (relative URL) skips it, staying on the same host.

verdict.summary: Off-by-one in the evidence-index guard: `idx <= area->evidence().size()` admits `idx == size`, and `area->deleteEvidence(idx)` at that index is out of bounds for the N-element evidence container.

evidence.reason: idx derives from attacker-controlled argv[0] via toInt (line 4) and its residual range after the guard at line 5 (`is_int && idx <= area->evidence().size() && idx >= 0`) is [0, N] because `<=` admits idx == N. deleteEvidence(N) indexes one past the last valid element (0..N-1) of the N-element evidence container, an out-of-bounds access/write (CWE-787). The Guard-Identity Audit passes (same value, same int type, no interleaved mutation) but the boundary operator is wrong; the absent one-statement fix is changing `idx <=` to `idx <` to exclude idx == N.

assumptions: area->evidence().size() is the element count N of the evidence container, so valid indices are 0..N-1.
deleteEvidence(idx) treats idx as a direct index into that container, per its name and the index-passing pattern.
limitations: The implementation of deleteEvidence is not shown; the out-of-bounds conclusion relies on standard index semantics of a container removal.

verdict.summary: No confirmed memory-safety vulnerability in the fragment. The auth-handshake path is covered by protective statements that pass the Guard-Identity Audit: buffer->size = buffer->pos (line 34) bounds the find_auth_end scan and the forwarded length to valid bytes; if (auth_end >= 0) (line 45) excludes the -1 sentinel that would turn buffer->size into SIZE_MAX and underflow extra_data = buffer->pos - buffer->size (line 49); if (extra_data > 0) (line 53) gates the g_bytes_new read (line 54), whose end pointer never exceeds the 64-byte capacity allocated at line 16. The D-Bus header path is guarded by if (required < 0) (line 74), and the body buffer allocated at line 81 is in-bounds by construction (capacity == required). The only residual concern — attacker-controlled required up to ~4 GiB reaching buffer_new — is a crash/resource-exhaustion DoS on attacker input and is recorded as a limitation, not a confirmed finding.

assumptions: buffer_new(size, parent) allocates a data buffer of exactly size bytes with size=size and pos=0, and g_malloc never returns NULL (standard GLib semantics).
buffer_read reads at most buffer->size - buffer->pos bytes at buffer->data + buffer->pos and increments buffer->pos (consistent with the pos <= size invariant used by lines 29 and 68).

find_auth_end returns the index of the NUL terminating the auth mechanism within the buffer's valid bytes, or -1; the shown statement buffer->size = buffer->pos (line 34) immediately before the call establishes size == pos, bounding the scan.
g_dbus_message_bytes_needed returns the total D-Bus message size (header + body) or -1 on invalid/too-short data; body_len is an attacker-controlled guint32 with no shown cap.
got_buffer_from_side forwards buffer->size bytes, which the shown assignments keep within each buffer's capacity (pos <= 64 for the auth buffer, required for the body buffer).
limitations: Unbounded allocation: required from g_dbus_message_bytes_needed (line 73) can be up to ~4 GiB via the attacker-controlled body_len and reaches buffer_new (required, buffer) (line 81) with only the negative check (line 74); the consequence is g_malloc abort / memory-pressure DoS on attacker input, which is demoted to a limitation (crash-only DoS) rather than a confirmed memory-safety finding. The absent one-statement fix would be an upper-bound check on required.

The exact scan bound of the unshown find_auth_end is assumed from its name-implied semantics plus the shown size == pos initialization (line 34); if the callee scanned a fixed window beyond pos, an additional in-callee guard would be required, but that is outside the shown fragment.
side->header_buffer capacity is not declared in the fragment (set outside it); the body-buffer analysis holds by construction regardless.

side->extra_input_data is overwritten without consuming the prior GBytes when multiple auth ends occur (memory leak, not memory-unsafety), and the current_read_buffer is not unref'd when buffer_read fails (leak, not memory-unsafety).

verdict.summary: png_zalloc is the fixed counterpart: the overflow guard `items > PNG_UINT_32_MAX/size` (line 14) constrains the same items/size values used in the multiplication (line 19), preventing the 32-bit overflow that would corrupt the size passed to png_malloc (line 22). The PNG_1_0_X memset block is null-checked and bounded by num_bytes.

zlib's zalloc contract supplies a nonzero size (sizeof of internal structs); the line-14 division assumes size > 0.

No caller is shown, so items/size magnitudes cannot be externally driven; even absent the guard, a failure would require an attacker-controlled oversized allocation request.

The present if (!max_size) guard (L10-13) protects the zero-size OOB class but does not affect the confirmed info-disclosure sink.

verdict.summary: pcmk_process_exit contains no confirmed vulnerability. The respawn path is bounded by the MAX_RESPAWN guard (lines 18-20) which sets child->respawn = FALSE when respawn_count exceeds the limit, excluding those counts from the start_child sink. The respawn loop is bounded by the MAX_RESPAWN guard (lines 18-20); unbounded forking / resource exhaustion is excluded.
Any comparison-operator or active-child-count semantics of pcmk_child_active (line 36) are not visible in the fragment, so no claim is made about its return-value edge cases.

verdict.summary: extract_tar_to_path validates archive entry paths with is_path_safe only in a first pass, then re-opens and re-reads the archive in a second pass that constructs the output path and writes files without re-validating current_file. If the archive source yields different entries between the two passes (FIFO, device, or file replaced in the TOCTOU window), an absolute or ../ entry bypasses validation and is extracted outside dest_path.

evidence.reason: current_file (line 138) is attacker-controlled archive data read in the second pass and is consumed at line 140 to form the output path, then written via archive_write_header (line 144) and archive_write_data_block (line 157). The only is_path_safe guard (line 116) runs in the first pass over a separate read of the file (lines 114-122); the second pass re-opens tar_path (line 130) and never re-validates, so the guard constrains a different value/read than the sink consumes (wrong-target drift, class 3). An entry such as ../... or an absolute path appearing only in the second pass (TOCTOU / non-idempotent source) is admitted by every guard and enables arbitrary file write outside dest_path. The absent fix is a second-pass is_path_safe(current_file) validation before line 140.

assumptions: tar_path may be a non-idempotent source or may be replaced between the first-pass read (line 114) and the second-pass re-open (line 130), causing the two passes to yield different entries.
is_path_safe's checks (absolute '/' at line 172 and '..' components at line 180) are sound for the values they test in the first pass.
limitations: Exploitation requires the archive content to differ between the two passes; for a stable regular file, pass 1 validates every entry that pass 2 reads, so the traversal is not reachable.
A possible NULL dereference at line 172 (path[0]) when archive_entry_pathname returns NULL is a library-contract concern not evidenced in-fragment, so it is not reported as a confirmed finding.

verdict.summary: op_format() restores the pre-format saved_cursor into curwin->w_cursor without re-validating it after format_lines() deletes/shortens lines, leaving the global cursor out-of-range (lnum > ml_line_count or col beyond line length), which downstream editor code dereferences as an index → out-of-bounds access. Missing fix: check_cursor(); after the restore.

evidence.reason: The sink stores saved_cursor ((captured from user-controlled oap->cursor_start at L27) into the global curwin->w_cursor after format_lines() (L29, whose insertion/deletion is evidenced by the L57-58 comment and L37 line-count delta) without any validity check. Capacity ml_line_count is the same counter read at L5, recomputed at L37, and compared at L43; on the keep_cursor==TRUE path (L26,the “gw” operator), saved_cursor.lnum/col can exceed the post-format capacity ((lines joined/deleted, lines shortened)), so every later cursor consumer indexes out of bounds. The only adjacent guard (L34-35, cursor.lnum < ml_line_count before ++curwin->w_cursor.lnum) is wrong-target drift: it constrains the pre-restore cursor, the same field is overwritten at L46, and it never tests saved_cursor. verdict.summary: hfile_mem_get_buffer stores the signed pointer difference file->buffer - file->limit into *length. For any non-empty memory-backed hFILE where limit = buffer + L (L >= 1), this is -L, which implicitly converts to size_t as SIZE_MAX - L + 1, so callers receive a near-SIZE_MAX length for the buffer returned at line 10 and over-read the heap (heap over-read / information disclosure). evidence.reason: Sink line 8 stores the signed ptrdiff file->buffer - file->limit into a size_t. Residual range of the mem-backend pointers: limit - buffer = L with no shown minimum or cap, so any L >= 1 is admitted (degenerate witness L = 1 yields stored value SIZE_MAX). Guard at line 7 (if (length)) admits the witness — it verifies only pointer validity, not the value — and the dispatch guard at lines 2-5 is bypassed for backend == &mem_backend, with both guards evaluated before this sink (lines 2, 7 then 8). The presentation of a near-SIZE_MAX length alongside the heap pointer returned at line 10 feeds a caller that bounds reads/copies by it, causing an out-of-bounds heap read (CWE-125). The absent fix is the one-statement reorder to *length = file->limit - file->buffer;, which would yield L and exclude the wrap; its absence leaves the signed-to-unsigned negative-width conversion (CWE-195) as the confirmed mechanism at this sink.

assumptions: hFILE buffer/limit layout follows the name-implied standard semantics of this accessor: buffer is the base/current read position and limit is one-past-the-end of valid data, so the correct returned length is file->limit - file->buffer (line 8 computes the negation).
The caller consumes the returned length as the buffer size according to the function's public accessor contract (size-bounded read/copy of the returned buffer).
size_t/ptrdiff_t are 64-bit, giving stored value SIZE_MAX - L + 1 for L >= 1.
limitations: NULL file (line 2 dereference) is not a finding: no NULL producer for the parameter is shown inside the fragment.
The out-of-bounds read itself occurs in the unshown caller; the confirmed in-fragment mechanism is the signed-to-unsigned conversion of the negative length at line 8.
No loops, crypto, file, or injection sinks exist in the fragment; the if (length) guard correctly prevents a NULL-write and is not itself a flaw.

stfl::quote's implementation is not shown in the fragment; its escaping behavior is inferred from its name and the parallel in-fragment sanitization at line 12.
The return status of utils::run_interactively (line 22) is discarded; UI-only, no security consequence is demonstrated in the fragment.
No memory-safety, NULL-dereference, integer-overflow, or crypto operations are present in the fragment.

verdict.summary: Stack-based buffer overflows in FAAD2 frontend main(): unbounded strcpy/sscanf("%s") copies of attacker-controlled argv/optarg data into fixed 255-byte (aacFileName/audioFileName/adtsFileName) and 10-byte (dr) local buffers with no length validation.

evidence.reason: Stack-based buffer overflow (CWE-121): argv[optind] is entry-point data with residual length range 0..unbounded (the only guard, L180 if (((argc - optind) < 1) || showHelp), admits a missing length and constrains only index presence, not string length). strcpy writes strlen(argv[optind])+1 bytes into aacFileName[255] (capacity declared L19); a 255-byte argument writes 256 bytes. Missing fix: a length check (e.g. strlen(argv[optind]) < sizeof(aacFileName)) or bounded copy before line 195.

Stack-based buffer overflow (CWE-121): optarg for -o is entry-point data, unconstrained by the only guard if (optarg) (L66), which checks NULL, not length (wrong-target drift). strcpy writes strlen(optarg)+1 bytes into audioFileName[255] (capacity declared L20); a 255-byte optarg overflows. Missing fix: length check or bounded copy before line 69.

Stack-based buffer overflow (CWE-121): optarg for -a is entry-point data; the only guard, if (optarg) (L73), constrains NULL, not length. strcpy writes strlen(optarg)+1 bytes into adtsFileName[255] (capacity declared L21); a 255-byte optarg overflows. Missing fix: length check or bounded copy before line 76.

Stack-based buffer overflow (CWE-121): sscanf's unbounded %s writes a whitespace-delimited token plus NUL into dr[10] (capacity declared L82) while optarg is unconstrained entry-point data; a 10-character token writes 11 bytes. The '< 1' check runs after the write and tests the conversion count, not the buffer length (check-after-use), so it protects nothing. Missing fix: a field width such as "%9s".

Stack-based buffer overflow (CWE-121): sscanf's unbounded %s writes a token plus NUL into dr[10] (capacity declared L93) from unconstrained optarg (entry-point, -f); a 10-character token overflows. The '< 1' return check is evaluated after the write and constrains only the conversion count. Missing fix: field width "%9s".

Stack-based buffer overflow (CWE-121): sscanf's unbounded %s writes a token plus NUL into dr[10] (capacity declared L107) from unconstrained optarg (entry-point, -b); a 10-character token overflows. The '< 1' return check runs after the write and constrains only the conversion count. Missing fix: field width "%9s".

Stack-based buffer overflow (CWE-121): sscanf's unbounded %s writes a token plus NUL into dr[10] (capacity declared L121) from unconstrained optarg (entry-point, -l); a 10-character token overflows. The '< 1' return check runs after the write and constrains only the conversion count. Missing fix: field width "%9s".

assumptions: argv[] entries and getopt_long optarg are NUL-terminated C strings (standard main/getopt contract); argv[optind] is non-NULL because L180 guarantees argc - optind >= 1.
No hidden OS or in-fragment cap bounds argv/optarg string length below the 255- and 10-byte buffer capacities.
Local buffers aacFileName[255] (L19), audioFileName[255] (L20), adtsFileName[255] (L21), dr[10] (L82/L93/L107/L121) are the capacities for the overflow derivations.
format is guaranteed to be 1 or 2 at L215 by L99-100 plus the L180 exit, which makes the file_ext[format] index read (but not the strcat write length) safe.
limitations: L215 strcat(audioFileName, file_ext[format]) is not reported as a confirmed sink: exceeding audioFileName[255] requires file_ext[format] to be at least 1 non-NUL byte beyond a 254-byte base, and that length is not derivable inside the fragment.
L208 strcpy(audioFileName, aacFileName) shares the L195 failure: it can only overflow after L195 has already overrun aacFileName for the same witness (dependent undefined behavior, same root cause).

L238 fread return is discarded; on a short read, header bytes are uninitialized and compared at L243 / pushed via ungetc at L253-260. No security boundary or disclosure is visible, so this is robustness, not a finding.

Attacker-controlled aacFileName reaches stderr via faad_fprintf %s at L220/L233/L279; CR/LF/terminal injection into stderr is demoted because no log backend or security consumer is shown in the fragment.
L280 length/dec_length assumes dec_length != 0; IEEE float division by zero is defined behavior and is not treated as a finding.

verdict.summary: continue_send guards the chr write with `if (ibe->outlen == 0) goto check_reset;` and resets outpos/outlen consistently (lines 20, 32), so the write length `outlen - outpos` at line 8 is always >= 0 and outpos <= outlen. No shown statement produces a negative (huge size_t) write length; the only degenerate `outlen == 0` case is excluded from the write path. No confirmed vulnerability.

assumptions: `ibe->outbuf` has capacity >= 2 (lines 29-30 write indices 0 and 1); its size is not shown in the fragment.
`qemu_chr_fe_write` returns at most the requested length, so `outpos += ret` at line 11 keeps `outpos <= outlen`.
`outlen`/`outpos` are mutated only by this fragment (lines 11, 19-20, 31-32), preserving `outpos <= outlen` and `outlen==0 => outpos==0`.
limitations: An OOB read in qemu_chr_fe_write via a negative `outlen - outpos` (line 8) is not demonstrable: it would require `outpos > outlen` or `outlen==0` with `outpos>0`; the former is not produced by any shown statement and the latter is excluded by the line 4-6 guard.
The `outbuf[0]`/`outbuf[1]` writes at lines 29-30 cannot be confirmed as OOB because the buffer capacity is not shown.
A negative/zero `ret` from the chr write (lines 10-16) only causes a timer-based retry with no memory-safety consequence.

verdict.summary: In dprintf_formatf(), a `%.*d` precision taken from the vararg list is stored into `prec` with only a negative-to-(-1) normalization (L122-125), leaving every positive long admissible. In the FORMAT_INT zero-padding branch, `while(prec-- > 0) *w-- = '0';` (L207-208) writes `prec` bytes below `workend` (L32) with no bound against `&work[0]` of `char work[BUFFSIZE]` (L25): a precision of 500 (or LONG_MAX) writes before the array — a stack buffer underflow (CWE-787). The one-statement protective fix, an added bound `while(prec-- > 0 && w >= work)`, is absent; the only capacity-relative guards (L359-360, L369-377) protect the FORMAT_DOUBLE sprintf sink, not this integer path.

evidence.reason: Sink is the integer zero-padding loop writing into `char work[BUFFSIZE]` (L25), starting from `char *workend = &work[sizeof(work) - 2]` (L32). `prec` derives from the vararg slot `prec = (long)vto[p->precision].data.num.as_signed;` (L119) for `%.*d`; the only guard is `if(prec < 0) prec = -1;` (L122-125), so any `prec >= 0` up to LONG_MAX is admitted (L188-189 excludes only -1, L198 subtracts only the digit count, L205 `prec > 0` admits the witness). With `prec = 500` (or LONG_MAX), the loop executes `prec` decrementing writes with `w` advancing below `&work[0]` after ~`sizeof(work)-2` iterations, i.e. an out-of-bounds stack write before the array — CWE-787. Guard-Identity Audit: the capacity-relative guards L359-360 and L369-377 are in FORMAT_DOUBLE (wrong-target drift class 3) and never constrain this FORMAT_INT path; no statement bounds the write count against `w >= work`. Absent one-statement fix: add the bound `w >= work` to the loop condition of L207.

assumptions: `work` is an array of `BUFFSIZE` bytes (declared L25) and `workend` (L32) points to its penultimate byte, so ~`sizeof(work)-2` zero-writes are the maximum that stay inside the object.

`vto[]` entries, including `data.num.as_signed`, are populated from the caller-supplied varargs by `dprintf_Pass1` (invoked and checked at L35-36), and `FLAGS_PRECPARAM` is set for `%.*`-style precision specifications.
`mp_uintmax_t` is a fixed-width unsigned integer (64-bit), bounding the digit loop (L193-196) to 64 bytes.
limitations: The `BUFFSIZE` constant value is not shown in the fragment, so the witness is a range (precision 500 / LONG_MAX); the existence of the out-of-bounds write is certain since LONG_MAX is admitted and exceeds any feasible array span, but the exact underflow byte count is not derivable in-fragment.
Bounds of `vto[param]` (L99) and `endpos[]` (L423) depend on unshown `dprintf_Pass1`/`dprintf_DollarString` validation and were not confirmed as a finding.

The FORMAT_DOUBLE path (S5) is protected by the shown width/precision caps (L359-360, L369-377) for non-degenerate doubles; edge cases such as negative-`prec` after clamping and width-vs-precision interplay (later upstream hardening) were not demonstrated to overflow from the shown statements.

verdict.summary: continue_send is the fixed counterpart: the chardev write at lines 7-8 and the outbuf writes at lines 25-26 have no in-fragment derivable failing value (outpos is bounded by outlen via the write contract and the shown resets; outbuf capacity is not shown), the retry cycle is terminated by the strict comparison at line 9 (excludes outpos == outlen), and the reset cycle is terminated by send_reset = false at line 29 (excludes a persisting send_reset). Hypothetical failures relying on a negative qemu_chr_fe_write return or an unshown buffer capacity are demoted to limitations.

assumptions: qemu_chr_fe_write returns at most the requested length (standard chardev contract), so outpos <= outlen is maintained on every shown path (line 7 consumes the return, lines 16/28 re-initialize outpos to 0).
The reset message writes at lines 25-26 target an outbuf with capacity >= 2; the buffer declaration is outside this fragment and cannot be verified here.
Between retry iterations the function returns and the timer yields the main loop; the only in-function cycle is the single goto send at line 31.
limitations: A negative return from qemu_chr_fe_write (line 7) would corrupt outpos and could produce an out-of-bounds pointer/length at lines 7-8, but the outpos type and outbuf capacity are not shown, and the -1 outcome is an assumed magnitude, not a demonstrated producer; with an unsigned 8-bit outpos the wrap self-heals through the line 9 comparison. Demoted per the OOB/status confirmation rules.
The outbuf[0]/outbuf[1] writes at lines 25-26 cannot be confirmed as out-of-bounds because the object's capacity is not declared or computed within the fragment.
A chardev that returns 0 indefinitely leaves the 10 ms retry cycle (lines 9-12) active indefinitely; this is treated as designed backpressure/retry semantics, not a confirmed non-termination finding.
Producers outside the fragment (e.g., the command handler that sets outlen/outpos for new messages) are not analyzed.

verdict.summary: In the FORMAT_DOUBLE branch, attacker-influenced width and precision (long, full domain, no shown cap) are serialized into the 32-byte stack array formatbuf via curl_msnprintf. The only guards, `width >= 0` (line 358) and `prec >= 0` (line 364), admit the failing values, and the size budget `left` is stale (snapshotted at line 332 before flag writes and not decremented for the precision NUL at lines 366-367), so a format such as %9223372036854775807.9223372036854775807f writes one byte past formatbuf[31] at line 366 and further past at lines 377/379. No bounding or sanitization statement covers this sink, so the decisive protective fix is absent.

evidence.reason: Stack OOB write (CWE-787) into `char formatbuf[32]` (capacity declared line 330). `prec` originates from `p->precision` (line 343, format-digit-derived `long`, full domain with no shown cap) and `width` from `p->width` (line 337); guards `width >= 0` (line 358) and `prec >= 0` (line 364) admit LONG_MAX, so witness `%9223372036854775807.9223372036854775807f` passes both in order. Width block writes 19 chars + NUL at indices 1..20 (line 360), fptr=21, left=31-19=12 (lines 361-362), but true capacity remaining is 32-21=11 bytes: `left` was snapshot at line 332 (32-strlen("%")) before flag writes shifted fptr (lines 347-354) and is decremented only by `len` which excludes the NUL byte — transformation drift (class 4). `curl_msnprintf` writes 11 chars + NUL = 12 bytes at indices 21..32, exceeding formatbuf[31]; lines 377/379 then write beyond it. Absent fix: a bound on width/precision, or `left` recomputed as `sizeof(formatbuf) - (fptr - formatbuf)`, or an early exit when fptr reaches formatbuf+32.

assumptions: The format string (line 6) is the function's entry-point input: it is parsed by dprintf_Pass1 (line 35) and scanned at line 42, and no shown constraint caps width/precision magnitudes.
curl_msnprintf has standard bounded-write semantics: at most size-1 characters plus a NUL terminator written at the target pointer.
A long value's decimal representation is at most 19 digits (LONG_MAX = 9223372036854775807), used in the arithmetic chain to line 366.
The dprintf_Pass1 failure check (lines 35-36) bounds spec-count/parse errors only; it does not bound p->width/p->precision values.
limitations: Line 383 `(sprintf)(work, formatbuf, p->data.dnum);` is an unbounded write into `char work[BUFFSIZE]` (line 25) for any precision >= ~BUFFSIZE (e.g. %.1000000f), but BUFFSIZE's numeric magnitude is not shown, so this is treated as an assumed-magnitude limitation rather than independent evidence.
Lines 205-208 (`while(prec-- > 0) *w-- = '0';`) can write below work[0] when prec > ~BUFFSIZE; same symbolic-BUFFSIZE caveat, kept as a limitation.
Line 99 `p = &vto[param];` with a large positional spec (`%N$`) has no shown bound; MAX_PARAMETERS's value and dprintf_Pass1's positional validation are unshown, so no OOB read is confirmed.
No NULL-dereference finding: `%s` is NULL-checked at line 258 and no in-fragment NULL producer exists for the FORMAT_INTPTR pointer writes (lines 391-401).

verdict.summary: The fragment's only input-derived allocation (buffer_new at line 89) is protected by the return-status check `if (required < 0)` at line 82, which excludes every negative g_dbus_message_bytes_needed outcome before the size is consumed. The auth-path copy at line 54 is bounded by `buffer->size = buffer->pos` (line 34), the `auth_end >= 0` check (line 45), and the `extra_data > 0` check (line 53), keeping the source range inside the 1/64-byte buffer. All buffer_read/parse/forwarding statuses are checked or fail-closed, and log writes use constant format strings. No failing value reaches a security-relevant sink.

assumptions: buffer_read fills at most (size - pos) bytes and returns FALSE on EOF/error, so pos never exceeds the capacity of the 1-byte (line 14), 64-byte (line 16), or required-sized (line 89) buffer.

find_auth_end searches the valid region [0, buffer->size) set at line 34 and returns a found end index within [0, pos], or -1 / FIND_AUTH_END_ABORT; no in-fragment statement produces an index greater than pos.
g_dbus_message_bytes_needed returns -1 (with error) for an invalid/incomplete header and otherwise returns the exact needed size (>= 16) after validating lengths against gsize.
buffer_new/g_malloc never returns NULL (GLib contract), and side->header_buffer capacity is at least the fixed D-Bus header size.
limitations: An attacker-controlled valid D-Bus header can make `required` at line 89 as large as ~4 GiB; the worst outcome is an OOM abort of the proxy process (crash-only DoS with no security-relevant state change), which the class rules treat as a limitation, not a finding.
If find_auth_end ever returned an index > pos, line 49 would underflow and line 54 would overread; no shown statement produces such a value, so this is unconfirmed out-of-scope behavior.

Buffer ownership across separate callback invocations (e.g., the refcount consequence of removing the line 22 condition) is not demonstrable inside this single invocation, so no use-after-free is confirmable from the fragment.
